axes.model_access:
**Officially self-described as model-agnostic**, listed as one of four principles in the README.

**Official wording**:
"Model-agnostic — works with any LLM that supports tool calling: frontier, open-weight, or local"

The FAQ elaborates: any model supporting tool calling works. Including:

- frontier APIs (OpenAI / Anthropic / Google)
- provider-hosted open weights (Baseten / Fireworks)
- models **self-hosted via Ollama / vLLM / llama.cpp**

The integration path is any LangChain chat model. **Switching providers requires no agent-code changes.**
axes.runtime:
**It is a library, not a service — you operate the process yourself.**

The README states it is built on LangGraph (streaming, persistence, checkpointing).
LangSmith can additionally be configured for tracing/evaluation/deployment.

**Responsibility split of the agent loop**:

- model decisions and tool calls run on the LangGraph runtime
- Deep Agents presets planning, context management, sub-agent delegation
axes.local_files:
**Filesystem capability is the core selling point**: read / write / edit / search.

Its backends are **pluggable** (pluggable local, sandboxed, or remote backends).
The official docs also have a standalone Sandboxes page covering isolated execution environments and the `execute` tool
(`SandboxBackendProtocolV2`; only sandbox backends expose a shell).

**Important boundary**: the official security statement says verbatim
"**Enforce boundaries at the tool/sandbox level, not by expecting the model to self-police**".

That is, the official docs explicitly do not provide a permission-guardrail layer; boundaries must be implemented by you at the tool/sandbox layer.

**Not stated officially**: conflict handling when multiple agents concurrently write the same file (overview / backends pages checked).
axes.background:
Self-hosted = **stops when stopped**, no hosted execution option (the README makes no such promise).

**But resume-after-crash has official support**:

- built on LangGraph's persistence + checkpointing
- persistent memory (pluggable state and store backends for cross-session recall)

LangSmith separately provides deployment officially.
axes.tools:
**The toolchain is positioned "batteries-included."** Officially listed capabilities:

- Sub-agents — delegation with isolated sub-contexts
- Filesystem
- Shell access (run commands in your sandbox of choice)
- Skills — reusable behaviors loaded on demand
- Tools — your own functions or **any MCP server**

**MCP support is explicit**: the official docs list "bring your own functions or any MCP server".

Human-in-the-loop: tool calls can be approved / edited / rejected, happening **before execution**.
axes.context:
**The textbook case of this track's "state ≠ context" distinction.**

- Context management = summarize long threads and **offload tool outputs to disk** (offloading, not discarding)
- Persistent memory = pluggable state and store backends, **supporting cross-session recall**

The official description: defaults are tuned for **long-horizon, multi-step work**.

Two practices coexist: compressing history + landing large tool outputs on disk + cross-session memory.
axes.permissions:
**The official docs explicitly do not defend against model overreach.** Security section wording:

**Official wording** (three sentences quoted together): "Deep Agents follows a "trust the LLM" model." "The agent can do anything its tools allow." "Enforce boundaries at the tool/sandbox level, not by expecting the model to self-police."

Meaning: it follows a "trust the LLM" model; the agent can do anything its tools allow.
Boundaries must be enforced at the **tool/sandbox layer** — do not expect the model to self-restrain.

**The only built-in human intervention point** is this:

human-in-the-loop tool-call approval (approve/edit/reject).

This means: after installing Deep Agents, the permission model is **your responsibility**.
axes.fit:
**Fits** three scenarios.

Wanting an out-of-the-box, well-tuned-by-default general Agent for long-horizon multi-step flows.
Not wanting to assemble filesystem / memory / sub-agents yourself. Already in the LangChain ecosystem.

**Does not fit** three scenarios.

Needing fine-grained permission guardrails — the official docs say they do not provide them; you must build your own sandbox.
Wanting strict control of the agent loop shape — use LangGraph custom graphs.
Wanting a lightweight harness — use LangChain `create_agent`.

sections.三层定位（本分区最需要讲清的一件事）:
This is the easiest thing to mix up: Deep Agents, LangChain, LangGraph are **three layers**.

The three layers have different responsibilities.

The official FAQ directly answers a question: what is the difference among the three?

Asked about LangGraph vs LangChain, the official docs break the relationship down clearly.

| Layer | What it is | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **LangGraph** | graph runtime (the lowest orchestration layer) | the agent loop shape is wrong for you and you need a custom graph |
| **LangChain `create_agent`** | minimal agent harness | wanting a lighter harness without preset middleware |
| **Deep Agents** | on top of `create_agent`, presets filesystem / sub-agents / context management / skills | wanting a complete harness out of the box |

The three-layer relationship, official wording:

> LangGraph is the graph runtime. LangChain's `create_agent` is a minimal agent harness on top of it. Deep Agents is a more opinionated harness on top of `create_agent` — same building blocks, but with filesystem, sub-agents, context management, and skills bundled in.

**The official docs also give the selection rule** (this is directly this site's selection answer):

> Use **Deep Agents** when you want the full harness — planning, context management, delegation — out of the box. Use [**LangChain's `create_agent`**] when you want a lighter harness without the bundled middleware. Drop to [**LangGraph**] when the agent loop itself isn't the right shape and you need a custom graph.

**Composability**: the official docs state any LangGraph `CompiledStateGraph` can be passed to a Deep Agent as a sub-agent.

So it is not either/or. **You can base on Deep Agents and use LangGraph graphs as sub-agents**.
sections.⚠ 最需要注意的一条：官方把安全责任交给你:
Security section wording:

> Deep Agents follows a "trust the LLM" model. The agent can do anything its tools allow. Enforce boundaries at the tool/sandbox level, not by expecting the model to self-police.

**This is not marketing language; it is a risk statement.** After installing:

| Officially provided | Officially not provided |
|---|---|
| human-in-the-loop tool-call approval (approve / edit / reject before execution) | any permission guardrail beyond the sandbox boundary |
| pluggable sandbox backends (**but you draw the boundary**) | model self-restraint |

**Practical conclusion**: wanting to use it while worrying about overreach, **you must tighten the sandbox yourself**.

Do not assume safety is in place just because **"it supports human-in-the-loop"**.
sections.\"状态 ≠ 上下文\"：它同时用了三种手段:
| Means | Official wording | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| summarize long threads | Context management | compresses long conversations |
| **offload tool outputs to disk** | Context management | **lands large tool outputs on disk instead of stuffing them into context** |
| persistent memory | pluggable state and store backends | **cross-session recall** |

The second item deserves special attention.

**Offloading** tool outputs to disk, rather than compressing them away.

This is closer to this site's stance on reliable long-running operation than simply "compressing history".

The official positioning is `defaults tuned for long-horizon, multi-step work`. The defaults are tuned for long tasks.
sections.模型支持：真的可以接本地模型:
FAQ wording:

> Yes. Any model that supports tool calling works — frontier APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), open-weight models hosted on providers like Baseten or Fireworks, and **self-hosted models via Ollama, vLLM, or llama.cpp**.

**This is key for this site**: the local quantized builds recommended by the model layer (models.specul.com) can also be connected.

See that site's series provider-compatibility notes.

**Suggested measurement** (per the five test dimensions specific to this site's harness section):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | How many files and lines a minimal hello agent takes | officially "batteries-included"; see how much the preset layer actually brings |
| 2 | Whether it can recover after interruption and where state is stored | officially promises persistence + checkpointing + persistent memory; the landing points need verifying |
| 3 | **Tighten the sandbox to the max and see what tools can still do** | the official docs hand boundary responsibility to users; this is the item most worth measuring |
| 4 | Two agents concurrently reading/writing the same directory | file-conflict policy not stated officially |
| 5 | How much changes when switching to an Ollama local model | officially model-agnostic; verify whether it really is zero-change |
